title: A queue that leaves work for later
dek: A validated batch limit caps the jobs in each send while keeping the remaining jobs in the pending queue.

sections.title: Each send took the whole queue
sections.content:
The worker previously treated everything waiting in the queue as one batch. On each tick, it drained the pending array and passed the result to send at the configured /jobs endpoint. The queue helper used pending.splice(0), which removed every entry from the beginning of the array.

That made the amount of pending work determine the size of each send. A short queue produced a small batch; a longer queue produced a larger one. There was no separate setting for how many jobs a single send should receive. PR #108 introduces that boundary between the queue and the worker.

sections.title: Waiting work is not a batch-size policy
sections.content:
Consider a pending queue with 250 jobs. Previously, the next tick handed all 250 to send. With the new default limit of 100, that tick takes the first 100 and leaves 150 pending. You can now configure the job count for each send independently of the queue's current length.

The split happens when the worker drains the queue. It does not create all future batches at once: the remainder stays available for later drains. The diagram shows that single-tick split, using the default setting.

{{DIAGRAM:0}}

The operational guarantee is deliberately narrow. You get a maximum number of jobs per send, not a promise about how expensive those jobs will be.

sections.title: Carry one validated limit into the drain
sections.content:
The configuration module establishes the limit before the worker uses it. It reads BATCH_LIMIT from the environment, defaults to 100 when the variable is absent, and converts the value to a number.

{{CODE:0}}

The guard runs when the module loads. Values such as zero, negative numbers, fractions, or nonnumeric text fail the positive-integer check and throw the stated error. An invalid setting therefore fails at startup rather than becoming a batch policy.

The queue helper applies that policy through the second argument to splice, which specifies how many entries to remove.

{{CODE:1}}

Removal still starts at the front of the array. The returned entries form this batch, and entries beyond the limit remain in the same pending array. If fewer jobs are waiting, the helper returns only those available.

The worker connects the setting to the helper and sends its result.

{{CODE:2}}

The configured value reaches the exact operation that removes jobs. We can follow the whole change from startup validation to bounded removal to the send call, without a separate batching loop.

sections.title: A count limit has a specific boundary
sections.content:
Job count, not resource usage

The author explicitly limits the guarantee to batch size. Counting entries provides the requested per-send bound, but it does not measure job memory or processing time. A batch of 100 jobs can still contain expensive work, and the jobs left pending still occupy the queue.

No tenant scheduling

Per-tenant scheduling remains out of scope because the queue has no tenant key. The helper takes the first entries in array order; it has no tenant identity on which to base a scheduling decision.

No stated follow-up plan

The supplied materials name no follow-up issue or priority order. These scope boundaries explain what this change guarantees today; they do not establish a commitment to resource-aware batching or tenant scheduling later.

sections.title: Three files connect policy to execution
sections.content:
All three changed files serve the same path: configure the count, apply it to pending work, and pass that bounded result to the sender.

FileWhat it does
config.tsDefines the default batch limit and rejects invalid configuration when the module loads.
queue.tsUses a removal count to return the first batch while retaining the rest of the pending array.
worker.tsImports the configured limit and passes it into the drain used by each send.

The supplied diff contains no test changes or test-run results. The walkthrough describes the behavior shown by the code, rather than a reported execution result.

sections.title: Send a bounded batch, retain the remainder
sections.content: PR #108 replaces whole-queue sends with a configurable job-count limit, defaulting to 100. Startup validation requires a positive integer, the drain removes at most that many entries, and the worker sends those entries while leaving the remainder pending. The result is a clear per-send boundary. It does not bound job memory or processing time, and tenant scheduling remains outside its scope because the queue lacks a tenant key.
